segments.original: The Vietnam War was the first war of the television age and produced striking images of the harsh reality of the battlefield. In contrast to World War II, however, Hollywood showed a distinct lack of enthusiasm for producing patriotic films. Usually cited as the only pro-war feature produced during the conflict, The Green Berets (1968) was savaged by critics for its simplistic stance.

segments.original: Hollywood films of the late 1960s and early 1970s tended to offer less direct reflections on the war. The insolent, anti-authoritarian tone of M*A*S*H (1970) had more to do with Vietnam than with its supposed setting, the Korean War. Ulzana's Raid (1972), a fascinating Western by Robert Aldrich (1918-1983), uses the story of a cavalry troop with the unhappy mission of recapturing a band of Apaches as a metaphor for a war that cannot be won.

segments.original: Authentic dramatizations of the Vietnam War had to wait until the fighting was over. segments.original: Chris Taylor (Charlie Sheen), who stands in for Stone, is an idealistic young man who volunteered to serve with the infantry in Vietnam. He feels torn between two "fathers": the gentle, sensitive super-soldier Sergeant Elias (Willem Dafoe), who smokes pot and listens to soul with the Black soldiers, and the sadistic, scar-faced Sergeant Barnes (Tom Berenger), who drinks and listens to country and western with the rednecks. Chris follows the path of other screen soldiers, "becoming a man", but whereas the recruits whipped into shape by John Wayne always ended up saluting the flag, Chris ends up losing faith in his country amid the blood and confusion.

segments.original: Although it is overly schematic in pitting the two sergeants against each other and contrasting their philosophies, Platoon is a powerful film. Terrifying as he is, Barnes teaches Chris how to survive rather than become a martyr - the climax, unthinkable in earlier films, has Chris shooting one of his own superiors rather than facing the enemy. Harrowing and suspenseful as it is, the film is not devoid of nostalgia - the soundtrack is made up of big 1960s hits and, in one scene, the soldiers sing "The Tracks of My Tears" by Smokey Robinson & The Miracles.

segments.original: Films dealing with America's emotional landscape in the wake of Vietnam provided an oblique commentary on the war. Who'll Stop the Rain (1976) shows a veteran and his best friend's wife on the trail of a shipment of Vietnamese heroin in California. The madness of the war is encapsulated in one of the film's lines of dialogue: "You see, in a world where elephants are pursued by flying men, people naturally want to get high."

segments.original: How can a shoot planned for 16 weeks end up lasting 15 months? In the case of Apocalypse Now, the real feat is that (almost) every member of the crew managed to finish the job alive. Its director, Francis Ford Coppola, ended up following his protagonist, Captain Willard, in his plunge into madness: if the soldier's mission was to hunt down Colonel Kurtz, Coppola's was to finish a film he had started without a screenplay and without an ending. He himself would admit to having contemplated suicide on three occasions over the four years of production, when everything that could go wrong went wrong. And everything nobody had even imagined could happen turned out even worse.

segments.original: No Hollywood studio wanted to hear about a film on Vietnam just months after the United States' defeat in the most controversial war in its history. Coppola secured the backing of the distributor United Artists, founded by Charles Chaplin (1889-1977) in 1930 so that artists would not have to depend on the commercial studios, but he was forced to negotiate personally with investors and back every loan with all his properties and the revenue still being generated by The Godfather (1972) and its sequel. In the '70s, Hollywood studios had not yet been absorbed by multinationals, so every dollar had to be negotiated. And shoots, thanks to the fact that executives were cinephiles rather than economists, could run long if the film deserved it.

segments.original: Apocalypse Now (released in the summer of 1979) was, according to cinematographer Vittorio Storaro (b. 1940), "a picture of the imposition of one culture on another and of the Americans' desire to turn everything into a spectacle": if real soldiers played rock and roll while bombing Vietnamese villages, the ones in the film listened to Wagner's Ride of the Valkyries. If the army devastated Vietnam with napalm explosions, Coppola would film the biggest explosion ever produced outside a war. With a budget of 11 million dollars (the same amount as Star Wars (1977)), Apocalypse Now would be the first art-house blockbuster.

segments.original: Steve McQueen (1930-1980) turned down the lead role, as did Al Pacino (b. 1940), Robert Redford (b. 1936) and Jack Nicholson (b. 1937). Frustration led Coppola to throw his five Oscars out the window and, after putting them back on the shelf, to hire Harvey Keitel (b. 1939). After three weeks of shooting, however, he realized that the actor's acting style did not suit a character who was supposed to function as a passive spectator on a journey to the end of the world and of the human soul. The replacement was Martin Sheen (b. 1940), who landed in the Philippines in the middle of his own battle with his demons: he drank nonstop, smoked three packs a day and, in one of the first scenes, collapsed on the floor screaming through tears. When he looked in the mirror and punched his reflection, his arm was covered in blood, but Coppola ordered the cameras to keep rolling while the actor screamed. Apocalypse Now had only just begun. The horror had not yet arrived.

The production was made in the Philippines because the country's president, the dictator Ferdinand Marcos, made everything easier: in exchange for thousands of dollars a day, the crew could use Philippine army helicopters and pilots and bomb as many hectares of forest with napalm as it needed. segments.original: On March 5, 1977, four days after the shoot passed the one-year mark, Martin Sheen woke up at two in the morning with unbearable chest pain. The actor left his tent and dragged himself along the road, in agony, for a kilometer until he found help. He was having a heart attack. When he heard, Coppola suffered an epileptic seizure, but he tried to hide the incident from United Artists. "Even if Martin dies, he's not dead until I say so," the director warned. Coppola had run up a debt equivalent to 135 million reais that would have left his wife Eleanor and his three children (Gio, 12; Roman, 10; and Sofia, 4) destitute. Suicide was no longer even an option.

segments.text: Apocalypse Now grossed five times its budget, which saved Coppola from bankruptcy, although his definitive ruin would come with One from the Heart, from nineteen eighty-two. Today, he says all the money he has is thanks to his vineyard in Napa, California. "The film isn't so strange anymore, seen today," the director reflected in twenty nineteen. "The same thing happened to it that happens to those avant-garde paintings that, over time, turn into wallpaper patterns."

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Marlon Brando, until the last day of his life (he died in 2004), complained that Coppola was "a fat bastard" who owed him two million euros (9 million reais). Apocalypse Now took so long to shoot that, in 1978, The Deer Hunter stole its honor of being the first Hollywood film about Vietnam. Before handing the Oscar to the director of The Deer Hunter, Michael Cimino (who would ruin his career two years later, also bringing about the closure of United Artists, with Heaven's Gate (1980)), Coppola took the opportunity to issue a warning about Hollywood that was met with scorn: the press ridiculed him, concluding that he had gone definitively mad because of the Apocalypse Now shoot. What was the aberration Coppola dared to prophesy? "Get ready, because digital technology is about to change cinema forever."
